items.title: Africa GNSS Lab Turns Its Launch Into a Working Plan in Tunis
items.description: Five months after the launch of the Africa GNSS Lab Academy in Sousse, the partners came together again to discuss the action plan.
content: Five months after the Africa GNSS Lab and the Africa GNSS Academy were launched in Sousse, the partners behind them came together again, this time to answer a more practical question: how does a shared vision become an institution that actually works? The second workshop took place in Tunis from 11 to 13 November 2026, on the sidelines of the SPACE STAR conference.

Over three days of presentations, debate and closed working sessions, participants focused on the two pillars of the initiative: research, development and innovation on one side and capacity building on the other. The aim was to validate a common strategic framework and gather enough input to finalise an operational roadmap. In other words, the workshop was less about announcing what the Lab wants to be and more about deciding how it will get there.

The room brought together a wide mix of backgrounds. Participants came from 14 African countries, from Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire and Burkina Faso in the west to Kenya and Tanzania in the east, with Italy also represented. Universities and research centres sat alongside start-ups such as GeoMinds Africa, Rada 360, Tod’Aers and Yoonir Smart Solution, and specialists in geodesy, remote sensing, artificial intelligence, precision agriculture, aviation and space law.

The SatNav Africa Joint Programme Office coordinated the sessions. Institutions including Senegal’s Université Amadou Mahtar Mbow and ASPG, Burkina Faso’s Institut Supérieur d’Études Spatiales et des Télécommunications, Tunisia’s Centre for Research in Microelectronics and Nanotechnology and Kenya’s Regional Centre for Mapping of Resources for Development led or contributed to different strands of the work. The attendees described this diversity as the network’s greatest asset.

The first day centred on the two committees. The Research, Development and Innovation Committee, led by Université Amadou Mahtar Mbow, set out a vision for the Lab as a hub for applied research, technology transfer and skills development. Its two-year action plan includes implementation of priority pilot projects, pan-African hackathons, innovation competitions and regular webinars, seminars and masterclasses.

The Capacity Building Committee presented the ambitions of the Academy, which will lead training across the network, from school pupils and university students to young professionals, decision-makers and trainers.

Participants endorsed both proposals in principle, with one message repeated throughout: research must answer real needs on the ground, whether those of communities, industry or local authorities. They also called for clearer indicators, stronger global navigation satellite system infrastructure and early outreach in schools. The day ended with an open roundtable on how academia, industry and government can work together.

On the second day, SatNav Africa shared the results of a survey of partners, the first attempt at an inventory of expertise across the network. It showed a multidisciplinary community with experience in training and in securing support from sources such as Erasmus+, Horizon Europe, the World Bank and the African Development Bank.

The discussion then turned to how the Lab will be governed and sustained. The Association Sénégalaise des Professionnels de la Géomatique (ASPG) presented a proposed structure with a Strategic Advisory Council and a permanent Executive Secretariat. Institut Supérieur d’Études Spatiales et des Télécommunications led the session on resource mobilisation, arguing that backers support projects with clear goals and measurable results. SWAN drew on its experience of Senegal’s global navigation satellite system reference stations, which have combined public and private support, and TGN suggested starting with a small portfolio of realistic projects.

The attendees were also candid about gaps. Representatives of Institut Supérieur d’Études Spatiales et des Télécommunications, the Regional Centre for Mapping of Resources for Development and Rada 360 noted that participation remains concentrated in North and West Africa, and urged the Lab to reach more of East, Southern and Central Africa.

The final day moved from strategy to practicalities. Rada 360, a precision agriculture start-up, showed how global navigation satellite systems and satellite data can support smallholder farmers, from mapping plots to guiding tractors, and offered its tools to the Lab’s pilot projects. The Kenya-based Regional Centre for Mapping of Resources for Development proposed acting as a regional focal point for the Lab and offered to host training events, share its e-learning platform and give partners access to data from its regional global navigation satellite system stations.

A large part of the day was devoted to the draft consortium agreement, which will bind public, private, academic and civil society partners and protect each member’s ideas and contributions. Participants agreed that Tunisia, through the Centre for Research in Microelectronics and Nanotechnology, could provide a solid legal and administrative foundation for the Lab. Participants also agreed to build communication tools, begin online training on existing partner platforms, and identify the first projects to launch.

The proposed roadmap starts with finalising the committees’ action plans and signing the founding and membership agreements before the end of the year. Early in the new year, the Lab is expected to launch its website and bring its Executive Secretariat into operation, ahead of the selection of the first projects.
For now, the message from Tunis is one of steady progress: partners are aligned on a shared direction, and there is a clear list of next steps to follow.

items.title: Disease Surveillance, Healthcare Staffing Top Public Health Budget Priorities
items.description: Muthoni urged the committee to consider interventions to address the funding deficit facing the State Department, warning that adequate financial support was necessary to implement its proposed programmes.
content: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Strengthening disease surveillance systems, addressing healthcare staffing shortages and improving sanitation are among the key priorities identified by the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards ahead of the 2027/28 financial year.

Principal Secretary Mary Muthoni outlined the priorities on Tuesday when she appeared before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Health to present the department’s proposals for the 2027 Budget Policy Statement.
The presentation, chaired by Committee Chairperson James Nyikal, focused on critical areas requiring additional investment to strengthen public health service delivery.
Muthoni highlighted the need to enhance disease surveillance and response capacity to ensure the country is better equipped to detect, monitor and respond to public health threats.
She also called for investment in Primary Health Care, improved sanitation and expanded access to essential public health services.

items.title: Gachagua skips Christmas as DCP machine shifts to top gear
items.description: Rigathi Gachagua assigns Senator John Methu grassroots mobilisation as DCP races to open offices nationwide ahead of Kenya's 2027 General Election.
content: Former Deputy President hands Methu the grassroots brief as Democracy for the Citizens Party races to open offices nationwide before 2027 primaries

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has assigned Nyandarua Senator John Methu the role of leading grassroots mobilisation for the Democracy for the Citizens Party, as Gachagua himself turns his full attention to preparations for the party’s primaries ahead of the August 2027 General Election.

The announcement, made on Tuesday, marked a deliberate shift in the operational structure of a party that has moved with striking speed since its formation. Methu, designated as the party’s Secretary General, had returned from a two-week break and was immediately handed one of the most demanding briefs in Kenyan opposition politics: opening DCP offices across all 47 counties and embedding the party in the grassroots networks that will ultimately determine whether Gachagua’s political project succeeds or stalls.

“This morning, I have welcomed Senator John Methu back to duty after a two-week rest,” Gachagua said. “Moving forward, the SG-designate will lead the team in officially opening all DCP party offices and driving grassroots political mobilisation, allowing me to focus on preparing for the party primaries.”

Methu’s response was characteristically direct. “Back to work,” he wrote. “A soldier reports to his commander after leave.” In four words, he captured something essential about the culture Gachagua is building inside DCP — disciplined, urgent and unapologetically militarised in its language of mission and sacrifice.

That sense of urgency is not performative. It reflects the brutal arithmetic of Kenyan electoral politics. The 2027 General Election is less than nine months away. Party primaries will precede it by several months, meaning the internal competition for DCP’s parliamentary and gubernatorial tickets is effectively already under way. For a party that is still establishing its physical infrastructure — offices, branch officials, registered members — the pressure to compress years of institution-building into months is immense.

Gachagua made clear that neither he nor his leadership team would be taking the festive season off. The party would observe only two days of rest — December 25 and 26 — before returning to the campaign trail. “Senator Methu, myself and our team will have no time for a Christmas break, except on 25th and 26th December,” he said. “The task ahead, to liberate our country from agents of corruption and impunity, leaves us no room for luxury.”

He went further, offering a promise that doubles as a campaign pledge: “My assurance is that, in December 2027, we will celebrate Christmas together and make up for the one we miss.” It is the language of a man who believes, with evident conviction, that the prize is within reach — and that the cost of reaching it is a holiday season spent in constituency meetings rather than around a family table.

The significance of this moment extends well beyond the internal mechanics of DCP. It speaks to the broader political realignment now reshaping Kenya’s electoral landscape in ways that have no precedent in recent memory. Gachagua’s removal from the Deputy Presidency through an unprecedented parliamentary impeachment in October 2024 was supposed to diminish him. It has not. If anything, it has clarified his purpose and sharpened his message, giving him the narrative of a wronged man fighting back — a story that resonates powerfully in the Mt Kenya region and is finding audiences beyond it.

DCP’s emergence has fundamentally complicated President William Ruto’s re-election calculations. The Mt Kenya vote bloc, which delivered Ruto his 2022 victory margin, can no longer be treated as a fixed asset. Gachagua is working methodically to peel it away, county by county, ward by ward, leveraging a combination of personal loyalty, regional grievance and an anti-corruption message calibrated to appeal to voters who feel the promises of 2022 have gone unfulfilled.

The decision to place Methu in charge of grassroots mobilisation is strategically sound. The senator brings credibility in the Mt Kenya North corridor, a network of relationships built over years in legislative politics and, critically, the energy of someone who appears genuinely invested in the project rather than merely attached to it for opportunistic reasons. His public response to the assignment — brief, soldier-like, devoid of self-promotion — will have been noted by party supporters as a sign of the seriousness with which DCP’s inner circle is approaching the task.

What DCP is attempting is, by any measure, ambitious. Building a party capable of mounting a serious presidential challenge in under two years requires not just enthusiasm but organisation: offices that function, branches that are legally compliant, members who are registered and motivated, candidates who are vetted and prepared, and a campaign infrastructure capable of reaching voters in every corner of a geographically and demographically diverse country. The opening of party offices across Kenya is not a ceremonial exercise. It is the foundation on which everything else rests.

The opposition landscape into which DCP is inserting itself is itself in flux. Former Prime Minister Raila Odinga’s death has reshuffled the political deck in ways that are still playing out, with his elder brother Oburu Odinga now leading the Orange Democratic Movement through a period of internal recalibration. Other opposition formations are watching the DCP surge with a mixture of interest and anxiety, calculating whether alignment or competition better serves their interests. Coalition conversations are happening, though few are conclusive. The shape of the opposition by the time campaigns formally open remains genuinely uncertain.

What is not uncertain is Gachagua’s intent. He has staked his political future, his reputation and apparently his Christmas on the belief that DCP can go the distance. The machinery is moving. The offices are opening. The Secretary General-designate has reported for duty.
Kenya’s most consequential election season in a decade has begun — and by all visible signs, the Democracy for the Citizens Party intends to be at its centre.

items.title: IEBC: No money to livestream 55,000 polling stations
items.description: IEBC Chair Erastus Ethekon rules out livestreaming Kenya's 55,000 polling stations in 2027, citing costs and logistics as election tensions rise.
content: Kenya’s election chief rules out full polling station broadcasts as 2027 campaign season ignites a fresh battle over electoral transparency

Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission Chairperson Erastus Ethekon has ruled out livestreaming proceedings at all 55,000 polling stations during the August 2027 General Election, citing prohibitive costs and insufficient time to procure equipment and train operators before polling day, in a disclosure that has sharpened an already fierce national debate over electoral transparency.

The admission, made at a consultative forum with the media, arrived at a moment of acute national tension. With the August 2027 General Election now less than nine months away, Kenya’s political temperature is rising fast. Coalitions are being tested, loyalties are shifting, and the institutions entrusted with delivering a credible election are once again at the centre of a storm that is as much about trust as it is about process. For millions of Kenyans who have lived through disputed elections, the question of who sees what, when, and how is never merely technical — it is existential.

Ethekon was unambiguous on the livestreaming question. The costs were too high, the logistics too complex, and the procurement timeline too tight. But he was equally firm on the broader question of transparency, insisting the Commission was concealing nothing and that courts had already settled the legal questions now being recycled as political ammunition.

The results declared at polling stations are final, he said. What follows — collation, tallying and verification at the National Tallying Centre — is administrative work required to determine whether a presidential candidate has secured more than half of all votes cast and at least a quarter of the votes in 24 or more counties. That is a constitutional requirement, rooted in Article 138 of the Constitution of Kenya. It is not, he insisted, a backdoor.
“I don’t understand what is all this fuss about the National Tallying Centre,” he said. “The courts have said the results at the polling station are final. The rest is secretariat work.”

The process, Ethekon maintained, would be conducted in full public view, with journalists, political party agents, international media, electoral observers and other stakeholders present throughout. Every stage would be open to scrutiny. “What more accountability are we asking?” he posed.

His words carry weight — but also carry the burden of history. Kenya’s elections have twice ended in catastrophic violence, in 2007 and 2017, with disputed results at their core. The scars have never fully healed. Each election cycle reopens the same wounds: who controls the count, who sees what, and whether the outcome reflects the will of the people or the will of those managing the machinery. It is against that backdrop that Ethekon’s assurances land, and against that same backdrop that they will be judged. Institutions in Kenya are not evaluated in a vacuum — they are evaluated against everything that came before them.

The political season now under way is unlike any Kenya has seen in recent years. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party is organising aggressively across the Mt Kenya region, reconfiguring loyalties that President William Ruto had long assumed were secure. Opposition figures are sharpening their messaging with renewed urgency. New alliances are forming quietly but deliberately, as politicians calculate which coalitions offer the clearest path to State House or, at minimum, to political survival beyond 2027. The election, analysts across the political spectrum agree, will be decided not only at the ballot box in August but in the months of mobilisation, narrative-building and institutional positioning that precede it — months that have already begun.

It is in that charged context that the debate over the National Tallying Centre must be properly understood. The centre has become a proxy battleground — a place where political actors raise doubts about electoral integrity without necessarily offering evidence of wrongdoing. The strategy is familiar: plant enough uncertainty in enough minds, and the legitimacy of whatever result emerges becomes contestable before a single vote is cast. Ethekon knows this dynamic well. His frustration was evident when he challenged politicians to provide factual information when discussing electoral processes, and urged journalists to move beyond simply amplifying what political personalities choose to say.

“Not just putting the cameras on their faces and allowing them to spill anything under the sun — some things that do not even make sense — and repeating lies,” he said, in remarks directed squarely at the media’s role in the information ecosystem surrounding elections.

He went further, alleging that some of the narratives circulating about the Commission and its processes were being deliberately manufactured by individuals and groups operating both inside and outside Kenya, with the specific aim of influencing public opinion and undermining national stability. The Commission, he said, would not allow unverified claims to go unchallenged, warning that sustained misinformation could discourage Kenyans from registering as voters or participating in the 2027 polls altogether — an outcome that would serve no democratic interest.

Commissioner Ann Nderitu sought to cut through the noise with a pointed question of her own: how would results from tens of thousands of polling stations be collated without a central facility? The question answered itself. She confirmed that Section 39(1G) of the Elections Act, which provides for the live-streaming of results announced at polling stations for public information, remains fully in force and unchanged. No media organisation, she said, has been barred from covering the process at any stage. Political parties that have not complied with requirements on their nomination rules have until December 7 to rectify their submissions, with December 9 marking the hard deadline for the closure of all public fundraising.

Commissioner Dr Alutalala offered what may have been the forum’s most grounding and, for some, sobering contribution — a direct challenge to the expectation that election results could be announced within an hour given the scale of Kenya’s electoral infrastructure and the manual nature of its processes. Kenya has approximately 55,000 polling stations spread across 47 counties, ranging from urban centres with reliable infrastructure to remote, hard-to-reach communities where logistics alone present enormous challenges. “We have 55,000 polling stations, our election is manual, and we are being told that within one hour election results should be announced,” he said. “Who bewitched us into believing that?”

The question was rhetorical. But it pointed at something deeply real: a widening gap between public expectation and operational reality that, if left unaddressed, becomes fertile ground for mistrust. Managing that gap — through honest communication, credible process and sustained public education — is now as important a task for the IEBC as the logistics of running the election itself.

Ethekon said the Commission would address this through sustained media engagement, regular briefings, information sharing and structured journalist training programmes designed to deepen understanding of how electoral processes actually work. A memorandum of understanding signed with the Kenya Media Sector Working Group provides the institutional framework for that cooperation, covering training and accreditation for coverage from individual polling stations all the way through to the National Tallying Centre.

Kenya’s history demands that every assurance be rigorously tested. Its future demands that every institution be given a fair and unobstructed opportunity to deliver. The IEBC is asking for both. Whether it earns them will depend not on the confidence expressed at media forums, but on what is seen — transparently, verifiably and without interference — when August 2027 finally arrives and every Kenyan vote must be counted and seen to count.

items.description: Safaricom’s Shiriki Pay lets M-Pesa users share wallet access with up to five beneficiaries, set KSh 20,000 monthly limits and keep full control of spending.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Safaricom has introduced a new M-Pesa feature called Shiriki Pay, designed to let customers delegate controlled spending access to people they trust, without the need to send money back and forth between accounts.
The service was unveiled on November 24, 2026, in Nairobi, targeting households, families and small businesses where financial responsibilities are commonly shared among multiple people.
To activate the service, an account holder, referred to as the sponsor, adds a beneficiary via My OneApp or the *334# menu, using the beneficiary's M-Pesa number and setting a monthly spending cap.

Each sponsor can register up to five beneficiaries, with individual monthly limits capped at KSh 20,000.
Once enrolled, a beneficiary can use the sponsor's M-Pesa wallet to make payments to Pay Bill numbers, Till numbers and Pochi La Biashara merchants.

However, they are restricted from withdrawing cash or accessing the sponsor's account balance and transaction history. Sponsors can adjust or revoke access at any point, maintaining full visibility over how funds are used.
Stephen Chege, group chief corporate and external affairs officer at Safaricom PLC, said the product responds directly to the realities of how Kenyan households and businesses handle money.

Safaricom positioned Shiriki Pay as part of its broader effort to expand M-Pesa's utility beyond conventional peer-to-peer transfers, offering customers a more structured way to manage shared expenses and support dependants or employees without relinquishing oversight of their accounts.

items.title: Hackers Steal Kenyans' ID Numbers, Other Details from eCitizen, US Firm Reports
items.description: ByteToBreach claims 740GB was stolen from Kenya's eCitizen platform, including identity documents. OAuth risks and links to agencies remain unconfirmed so far.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

A cybercriminal group operating under the alias "ByteToBreach" has claimed responsibility for stealing approximately 740 gigabytes of data from Kenya's national eCitizen platform, an allegation that has spread widely across Kenyan technology publications since Monday but remains unconfirmed by any government authority.

The claim first appeared on an underground data-trading forum on the evening of November 22, 2026, and was subsequently flagged by VECERT, a Miami-based private threat intelligence firm that monitors such platforms.

As of Tuesday afternoon, no statement had been issued by the Ministry of ICT, the national cybersecurity response team KE-CIRT/CC, the National Treasury , or the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner.

Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

According to VECERT's alert, ByteToBreach says it exfiltrated roughly 600GB of Know Your Customer (KYC) documents, which typically include copies of national identity cards and passports submitted by citizens, along with 100GB of government database records and 40GB of source code written in Erlang, Elixir, and Node.js.
Some files allegedly carried timestamps dating to November 14 and 15, 2026, though no data has been released publicly to support the claim.
The group alleges it gained initial access by exploiting a file-upload bypass vulnerability, which allowed it to deploy a webshell for remote code execution.
More critically, the post claims that eCitizen's OAuth and Single Sign-On (SSO) infrastructure was compromised.

The Social Health Authority, the Directorate of Criminal Investigations , Safaricom, and the National Police Service are named as potentially affected services due to their integration with eCitizen's identity layer, though no evidence has been produced showing those entities were directly accessed.
KNH announces closure of front section of International Trauma Centre for 120 days

Cybersecurity analysts have flagged the alleged compromise of OAuth signing keys as particularly significant. In a federated identity system, eCitizen issues digitally signed tokens that connected services accept as proof of a user's identity.

Should those signing keys have been stolen, an attacker could theoretically forge tokens and impersonate citizens or officials across multiple platforms without ever needing their passwords, making a simple password change inadequate protection.
VECERT recommended that technical teams rotate JWT and OAuth signing keys immediately, revoke all active tokens, and audit file-upload endpoints for webshells.
ByteToBreach is a financially motivated group believed to be linked to Algeria and active since at least June 2025.

Romanian and Hungarian authorities have tied the group to attacks on government systems, including Romania's national land registry, in July 2026. However, its claims have not always held up to scrutiny.

In November 2026, the group claimed to have stolen 70GB from NSW Health in Australia; police there assessed the actual volume at around 4GB and said no patient data was involved, with an officer describing the actor as "a nuisance" with a history of false claims.
Questions over push by some politicians for Smartmatic to supply Kenya's 2027 KIEMS Kits

The alleged breach follows a documented increase in attacks on Kenyan government infrastructure. The Communications Authority of Kenya's report covering July to September 2026 recorded approximately 2.696 billion cyber threat events, a 14.45% rise from the preceding quarter, with web application attacks up 57.62% and brute-force attacks up 85.41%.

Under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019, data controllers must notify the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner within 72 hours of confirming a breach involving personal data. No such notification has been made public.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 champions by CAS ruling
items.description: CAS unanimously reinstates Senegal as Afcon 2025 champions, overturning CAF's decision to award Morocco the title after the chaotic January final.
content: Court of Arbitration for Sport unanimously overturns CAF’s controversial decision to award Morocco the title after the chaotic Casablanca final

Senegal have been reinstated as Africa Cup of Nations 2025 champions after the Court of Arbitration for Sport unanimously upheld their appeal against the Confederation of African Football’s decision to strip them of the title and award it to Morocco following one of the most chaotic finals in the tournament’s history.

The Swiss-based sports court announced its verdict on Tuesday, confirming that Senegal’s original 1-0 victory after extra time stands, and that the title belongs to the Lions of Teranga — not the Atlas Lions. “The Court of Arbitration for Sport has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation against the Confederation of African Football and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025,” CAS said in a formal statement. The decision was unanimous.

To understand why this ruling matters, it is necessary to revisit what happened in Casablanca in January. With the final still goalless and tensions running high, the referee awarded Morocco a penalty. Senegal’s players, convinced the decision was unjust and incensed by what they believed was home-nation bias, walked off the pitch in protest. It was a dramatic, ill-disciplined moment — but a temporary one. The players returned. The match restarted. Senegal won 1-0 after extra time and celebrated what they believed was a historic continental triumph.

Then CAF intervened. In March, the confederation’s Appeals Committee overturned the result entirely, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title, citing Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations. Those articles state that if a team refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the referee’s authorisation, it shall be considered the loser and eliminated from the competition. It was a seismic decision — one that stripped a champion of its crown not on the pitch but in a committee room, and one that immediately drew fierce criticism from across the African football community.

Senegal’s federation went straight to CAS. Their argument was straightforward and, as it has now been confirmed, legally sound: the Senegalese players did not abandon the match. They returned to the pitch. The referee restarted the final. The game was completed. The result was produced on the field of play under the oversight of the match official. If the referee had determined that the conditions for resuming the match had not been met, the game would not have restarted. It did restart. That, the CAS panel ruled, was determinative.

The panel found that the referee’s decision to restart the final demonstrated that “the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” and therefore that Articles 82 and 84 were “not applicable in this case.” CAF had, in effect, applied rules designed for teams that abandon matches to a team that completed one. CAS corrected that error with a clarity that left no room for ambiguity.

The ruling has implications that extend beyond the two nations directly involved. It raises serious questions about CAF’s governance and its decision-making processes in high-stakes situations. The confederation’s March ruling was always legally fragile — the basic facts of the final, that the match was completed and a result was produced, made the application of abandonment regulations extraordinarily difficult to justify. That CAF pressed ahead regardless, in a decision that awarded the title to the host nation, was always going to face the most intense scrutiny at an independent tribunal.

For Senegal, the ruling restores not just a trophy but a sense of justice — and of narrative. The Lions of Teranga, who have long been among Africa’s most admired footballing nations, now hold the continental title they won on the pitch in January without qualification or asterisk. For their players, their federation and their supporters, the past several months have been defined by an injustice that is now formally corrected.
For Morocco, it is a painful reversal. The Atlas Lions had celebrated a home triumph. That celebration has now been officially undone.

African football’s governing body will need to do considerably more than accept the CAS ruling — it will need to explain how it reached a decision that a unanimous international panel has found to be wrong.

items.title: How Hackers Allegedly Stole 740GB of Sensitive Data From Kenya's eCitizen Portal
items.description: The government has urged Kenyans to change their eCitizen passwords and watch out for fraudsters following reports that hackers stole 740GB of sensitive records from the state portal. In a statement on Tuesday, Novemb…
content: The government has urged Kenyans to change their eCitizen passwords and watch out for fraudsters following reports that hackers stole 740GB of sensitive records from the state portal.

In a statement on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services warned that criminals could exploit news of the alleged breach to target users through fake phone calls, text messages, emails and links.
"Fraudsters may use them to target the public Dont share your password or one-time PIN (OTP) with anyone. eCitizen will never ask you for them," the department said.

Officials advised anyone who reuses their eCitizen password on other websites to switch to a strong, unique combination immediately. They also asked users to report suspicious account activity and rely only on official channels for updates rather than spreading unverified claims.

The warning comes after cybersecurity monitoring firm VECERT Analyser reported that a group calling itself ByteToBreach had breached the platform. The attackers claimed to have extracted 600GB of personal identification and verification documents, 100GB of government database records and 40GB of computer source code.

According to technical details from the report, the hackers gained initial access by exploiting a flaw in eCitizen's file-upload system. That vulnerability allowed them to run commands on the servers using a webshell, a malicious script that gives attackers remote control over a web server.

The intrusion also allegedly reached federated identity systems, the shared login infrastructure that lets Kenyans access multiple connected agencies using a single eCitizen account. Because of this link, the breach potentially exposed integrated entities including the Social Health Authority (SHA), the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and the National Police Service.

The State Department, which falls under the Ministry of Interior and National Administration headed by Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, said security teams are investigating the reports to determine the extent of the damage and whether any data actually landed in unauthorized hands.

"The State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services is aware of reports circulating online on unauthorised access to data on the eCitizen platform. The office is treating these reports seriously and the technical and security teams are investigating to establish the extent of the incident," the department said.
Despite confirming the security probe, the ministry maintained that the incident has not disrupted public access to the central government services gateway.

"We are working with the relevant government agencies to respond to the incident. eCitizen services remain available, and the public can continue to access government services as usual," the statement added.
The department promised to release further updates once technical teams conclude their investigation.

content: PSG have the chance to remain atop the Champions League table when they host AS Roma in the headline fixture on Wednesday night.
The back-to-back Champions League winners are unbeaten and have 12 points from their opening four games.
Barcelona, Liverpool and Sporting Lisbon are also all in action on Wednesday, looking to record positive results to remain in the top 10 position in the league phase.
With another nine matches scheduled to be played, we have a look at the top games and offer our predicted outcomes.

The hosts are in 31st place with three points ahead of the crucial match, knowing that defeat will definitely relegate them from the competition.
They have an uphill task against fifth place Barcelona who are seeking a fifth consecutive victory in all competitions.
Barca are coming off an impressive 3-2 comeback victory against Villarreal over the weekend, while Sabah were 2-0 winners against Kapaz in the Azerbaijan league.
Raphinha has scored six goals in his last four Champions League appearances and has 23 goals in his last 26 appearances in the competition.
The Brazilian and Lamine Yamal will be the main attacking outlets for the visiting team, who are tipped as favorites to win convincingly.
Prediction – Barcelona to win + Over 2.5 goals
This match pits two sides against each other with nothing to separate them in the Champions League this season.
Both teams come into the game with nine points and a similar goal difference (4) as they look to cement a qualification place.
The home team are in better form, unbeaten in their last 11 matches, confident they can get a positive result against the reds.
Liverpool will be boosted by their emphatic 4-0 win against Manchester United over the weekend.
Liverpool have scored 14 goals and conceded 10 in their first four league-phase games.
The 10 goals conceded are already their highest total after four Champions League group-stage/league-phase matches in club history.
The hosts have been poor in the Champions League and only have one point after four matches.
They face a 13th place Bayern Munich who have eight points as they seek to break into the top eight positions.
Lille have lost both games they have played against Bayern by a 7-1 aggregate scoreline back in 2012.
Bayern have scored at least twice in 12 of their last 13 Champions League matches.
Their last 10 Champions League games have produced 50 goals — exactly five per match on average.
Lille have also scored in their last nine Champions League home matches, and every one of those games has featured a first-half goal.
The holders have been supreme in the competition and are at the top of the standings with 12 points after a perfect start to the campaign.
Paris are unbeaten in their last 14 Champions League matches, winning 10 and drawing four.
That is a club record and equals Lyon’s French record for consecutive unbeaten matches in the competition.
PSG have scored 20 goals in their first four league-phase games, the highest total of any team at this stage. They also bring a 12-game winning streak to the game.
Roma have won only one of their last 11 Champions League away matches, while they have conceded in their last 33 away matches in the competition.
The home team are seeking a sixth straight win in all competitions when they host a struggling Man United on Wednesday.
Sporting have won their last five matches in all competitions and victory here will see them cement their qualification hopes.
United, who appointed Mauricio Pochettino, as their new manager suffered an embarrassing 4-0 defeat away at Liverpool over the weekend and are desperate for a positive result here.
The Red Devils are in 17th place with six points and must avoid defeat to keep any qualification hopes alive.
The last time these sides met was in the 2007 Champions League and United won both legs with a 3-1 aggregate score.

George Ruto’s 98 Matatu Undergoes Major Renovations after Accident, Photos Emerge
items.description: George Ruto’s Baba Yaga matatu was stripped at the front after its Ongata Rongai crash, with new photos hinting at a dramatic comeback and a fresh look.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
George Ruto's popular John Wick-themed nganya, Baba Yaga, is undergoing major renovations at a local garage.
Fresh photos show the extent of the transformation, with significant changes to its front section.
The images, shared with TUKO.co.ke by matatu enthusiast Brian Musili, show Baba Yaga parked in a dusty garage, barely recognisable from the front.
Ian Washika: Young politician's majestic Mumias home wows Kenyans
PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
The bumper, bonnet and grille have all been pulled off, leaving exposed wiring and bare metal in place of the sharp gold-and-black bodywork that made the vehicle a fan favourite.
The John Wick lettering on the windscreen and the orange Baba Yaga sticker remain intact, as do the rows of roof lights, with a technician in grey overalls visible beside the vehicle.
For anyone who has followed Baba Yaga's journey, the contrast with its former look is stark.
The nganya was previously known for its menacing black-and-bronze body kit, a grille with sharp vertical slats, sleek LED headlights, and three round red-rimmed lights running across the bumper.
Musili told TUKO.co.ke that Baba Yaga appears set for a major transformation, with technicians having already dismantled the front section fans knew and loved.
He drew comparisons to Matrix, rebranded as Zoro, another of George's matatus that returned with a fresh look after going in for repairs following an accident.
Eric Omondi starts building huge house for Bungoma boy with skin condition after raising KSh 10.2m
The nganya was involved in a crash earlier this month along the Ongata Rongai route, reportedly rear-ending fellow popular matatu Detroit after the two vehicles allegedly engaged in a road race .
The incident left Baba Yaga with heavy damage to its front bumper , bonnet, grille and left headlight area, while Detroit's rear section also took a serious hit.
No fatalities or official injuries were reported from the incident.
The following morning, the Baba Yaga crew, operating under Raptors and 98 Sacco, acknowledged the crash on Instagram without sugarcoating it.

It was not an isolated incident either. This crash was actually the second major accident involving Baba Yaga in roughly six weeks, suggesting the rebuild is as much about necessity as it is about giving the matatu a fresh identity.

TUKO.co.ke also highlighted George’s Mood matatu, which also recently underwent a major makeover at an industrial paint garage.
Its front was coated in lilac, while parts of the previous teal-and-green artwork remain visible.
The finished design was revealed days ago.

When a pig's kidney gives a human a second chance: The medical breakthrough that could change millions of lives
items.description: A US woman has lived a year with a genetically modified pig kidney, a milestone that raises hope for kidney patients and questions for countries like Kenya
content: Dialysis can keep patients alive, but it comes at a considerable physical and psychological cost. Patients often spend several hours connected to machines multiple times a week. Their lives become organised around hospital appointments, treatment schedules and the constant uncertainty associated with kidney failure. She can drive again. She can prepare meals for her family. She can meet friends and look forward to travelling to visit relatives. She is even contemplating returning to skiing.

items.title: Kenya: Principal Secretary (PS) Muthoni Presents 2027/28 Public Health Priorities to National Assembly Health Committee
Kenyans Get Court Relief Over 2% Health System Fee as Govt Faces 120-Day Deadline
items.description: The High Court found the 2% HIMS fee lacked adequate public participation but gave the government 120 days to fix it. Otherwise, the fee entry will lapse.
content: The High Court has ruled that the 2 percent Health Information Management System (HIMS) fee was introduced without adequate public participation, declaring the charge unconstitutional in a petition filed by Nakuru-based surgeon Dr Benjamin Gikenyi.

Justice Reuben Nyakundi found that the fee, listed in the Third Schedule of the Digital Health (Data Exchange Component) Regulations, 2025, breached Articles 10(2)(a) and 201(a) of the Constitution, as well as Section 5 of the Statutory Instruments Act.

However, the court suspended its declaration of invalidity for 120 days, giving the government time to address the procedural shortcomings. Justice Nyakundi said immediate invalidation could disrupt funding for a system that processes about 26,000 claims daily, potentially affecting health facilities and patients.

“That a declaration be and is hereby issued decreeing that there is ambiguity in the 2% HIMS system on this charge and the same ought to be revisited on grounds of non-public participation on key sector-wise stakeholders to establish how the 2% fee capped at Kshs 5000 was arrived at and whether it is intergenerational or is capable of being reviewed and at what terms,” the court ruled.
The court directed the regulation-making authority to subject the HIMS fee to public participation in line with the Constitution and the Statutory Instruments Act within the 120-day period.

Any proposed fee must also come with a regulatory impact statement explaining how the charge was calculated. If the government does not introduce a lawful fee entry within the deadline, the existing entry will lapse.

The court declined to order refunds for fees already collected. It said the charges had been imposed under a published legal instrument that was presumed valid and had not been annulled when the money was collected. It also noted that the fees had paid for services already provided and that refunding payments across hundreds of thousands of claims would be disproportionate to the procedural violation.
The judge questioned whether the 2 per cent fee had received the necessary Senate concurrence, given that the Constitution assigns health services to county governments under the Fourth Schedule.

The court directed State organs to take steps to meet their constitutional obligations and submit monthly progress reports to the High Court’s Deputy Registrar, under the advisory of the Attorney General.

It declined to issue guidelines on government institutions doing business with citizens, saying policy-making on the matter fell outside the court’s role. However, it noted that the Auditor General has an independent constitutional mandate to audit the Department of Health’s accounts, including revenue collected through the HIMS fee.
The court also said personal liability under Article 226(5) would require proof that the unlawful use of public funds caused a loss. The petition had not established such a loss.

The ruling also addressed public institutions’ appointment of private advocates. The court held that law firms engaged by public institutions and county governments do not enter purely private contractual arrangements because those engagements carry a public element.
As a result, such appointments must comply with principles of fairness, transparency, non-arbitrariness, and equal opportunity.
The government now has 120 days to address the legal and procedural concerns surrounding the HIMS fee. If it fails to do so, the current fee entry will lapse.

items.title: KNH health workers down tools over delayed salaries
items.description: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Health workers at Kenyatta National Hospital have protested over the alleged failure by the institution to remit money deducted from their salaries for pension contributions,…
content: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Health workers at Kenyatta National Hospital have protested over the alleged failure by the institution to remit money deducted from their salaries for pension contributions, insurance premiums and loan repayments.
The employees staged demonstrations outside the hospital, as they protested delayed salaries, partial payments and unresolved welfare concerns.

The workers accused the hospital management of withholding or failing to forward deductions made from their payslips to the respective statutory bodies, financial institutions and third-party lenders.
The concerns have triggered an industrial dispute, with the employees downing their tools to demand urgent intervention by the hospital’s administration.
The Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union has since issued a 72-hour ultimatum to KNH management to address the grievances.
